opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the hardest part is that you're designing for a behavior that doesn't fully exist yet. With something like Canvas, we weren't just building a new interface. We were asking: what does it actually look like for a person and a model to collaborate on a piece of writing or code, rather than just trading messages back and forth? There's no established playbook for that.

Part of it is a modeling problem. The model has to learn *when* to open a canvas and when to just answer in chat. It has to know when to make a targeted edit versus rewrite the whole thing, and how to leave inline comments that are actually useful instead of noisy. Those are subtle judgment calls. If you get them wrong, the feature feels intrusive or dumb, even if the underlying model is very capable.

Then there's evaluation, which I think is underrated as a challenge. With a lot of product behaviors, you can't just look at a benchmark number. You need evals that capture things like "did this edit preserve the user's voice" or "was triggering the canvas the right call here." A lot of that ends up being a mix of human judgment, carefully designed synthetic data, and iterating on what "good" even means.

And finally, it's the tight loop between research and product. You're shipping something where the model behavior *is* the product. So the researchers, designers, and engineers have to work very closely, and you have to be comfortable with a lot of ambiguity early on. You prototype, you put it in front of people, you realize your assumptions about how they'll use it were wrong, and you go back and retrain or rethink. That cycle is both the hardest part and, honestly, the most fun part.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hardest part is that there's no playbook. With something like Canvas, you're not just shipping a UI, you're trying to figure out what collaboration between a person and a model should even feel like. There's no prior art to copy.

So most of the difficulty is in the early phase where you have to answer very fuzzy questions. When should the model make a targeted edit versus rewrite the whole thing? When should it open the canvas on its own versus wait to be asked? Those sound like small product decisions, but they're actually model behavior decisions, and getting them wrong makes the whole thing feel either intrusive or useless.

And that's the second hard part: the product and the model are the same thing now. In traditional software you design the interaction and then build it. Here, the model's behavior is the interaction, so you end up doing research and product at the same time. You write evals, you generate synthetic data, you train on it, you look at outputs, you notice the model is triggering canvas way too often for casual questions, and you go back and fix that. It's a very tight, very messy loop between researchers, designers, and engineers who are all reasoning about the same thing from different angles.

The last piece is taste. A lot of this comes down to judgment calls that are really hard to measure. What makes an edit feel like a thoughtful collaborator versus a tool that did what it was told? You can get metrics on trigger accuracy, but "does this feel good to work with" is something you mostly learn by using it yourself for weeks and being honest about what annoys you. That part never gets automated away.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part is figuring out what the interaction should feel like when the model can do so many different things. With something like Canvas, when should the assistant edit directly, when should it leave a suggestion, and when should it ask you a question? Those choices really affect whether you feel in control.

And the model behavior and the interface have to work together. You can have a very capable model, but if it changes more than you expected or interrupts your workflow, it doesn’t feel helpful. So the challenge is turning that capability into something you can understand, steer, and trust.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part is figuring out what the interaction should feel like when the model can do so many different things. With something like Canvas, you have to decide when the model should respond in chat, when it should edit the document directly, and when it should ask you a question. Those choices really shape whether it feels like a useful collaborator.

And the model behavior and the interface are very connected. You can build a great interface, but if the model rewrites everything when you only wanted one sentence changed, the experience breaks. So a lot of the challenge is making those two pieces work together, while giving the user enough control to trust what’s happening.
